I dunno how to put it... deconstructing what you're seeing on screen, since you're seeing real people actually moving, but then you're seeing it all through the lens of interpretation that a layer of rotoscoping adds to it.

Nietzsche was at least somewhat informed by Buddhism and discussed it in his works. He was a pupil of Schopenhauer who is often credited as something of a pioneer in discussing eastern thought in western philosophy. In *Beyond Good and Evil*, Nietzsche expresses a certain appreciation for Buddhism (stating that it latches onto an essential dimension of what it is to be human) while decrying what he saw as a certain nihilistic aspect of “self negation.”

Nietzsche felt that the observation “there is no true self” should be a call to self creation. Whereas Buddhists, to him, withdraw from life due to this understanding, he thought we should forge ahead even more strongly. In *Truth and Lies in the Non-Moral Sense*, he talks about treating the human mind as a scaffolding, a structure that we can freely create and recreate.

So indeed, the movie is very much a reflection of the philosophy it name drops. The Buddhist connection is “incidental” in a sense, but also an on point observation. Nietzsche saw himself as grappling with the same questions as Buddhists (among others of course) while coming to starkly different conclusions.
I've currently watched Dazed and Confused, Before Sunrise, and Before Sunset.......there's Buddhist philosophy everywhere. I completely understand now why my question may of seemed bizarre hahah.
